public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Normality of Irrational Algebraic Numbers

It is unknown whether every irrational algebraic real number is normal in any integer base.
Here a real number is *normal in base* $b$ if, for every $k \ge 1$, every string of $k$ digits
appears in its base-$b$ expansion with asymptotic frequency $1/b^k$.
The stronger conjecture that every irrational algebraic real number is absolutely normal is stated
separately: normality in one base and normality in every base are not equivalent definitions.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia: Normal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number)
- [BC01] Bailey, David H., and Richard E. Crandall. "On the random character of fundamental constant
  expansions." Experimental Mathematics 10.2 (2001): 175-190.
  https://projecteuclid.org/journals/experimental-mathematics/volume-10/issue-2/On-the-random-character-of-fundamental-constant-expansions/em/999188630.full
-/

@[expose] public section

open NormalNumber

namespace AlgebraicNormality

/-- A real number is irrational algebraic if it is algebraic over `ℚ` but not rational. -/
def IsIrrationalAlgebraic (x : ℝ) : Prop :=
  IsAlgebraic ℚ x ∧ Irrational x

/-- The strong normality conjecture: every irrational algebraic real is absolutely normal. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11 12 41]
theorem irrational_algebraic_absolutely_normal :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ x : ℝ, IsIrrationalAlgebraic x → IsAbsolutelyNormal x := by
  sorry

/-- The weaker normality conjecture: every irrational algebraic real is normal in at least one
integer base `b ≥ 2`. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11 12 41]
theorem irrational_algebraic_normal_in_some_base :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∀ x : ℝ, IsIrrationalAlgebraic x → ∃ b : ℕ, 2 ≤ b ∧ IsNormalInBase b x := by
  sorry

/-- Absolute normality implies normality in at least one base. -/
@[category API, AMS 11]
theorem normal_in_some_base_of_absolutely_normal {x : ℝ} (hx : IsAbsolutelyNormal x) :
    ∃ b : ℕ, 2 ≤ b ∧ IsNormalInBase b x :=
  ⟨2, le_rfl, hx 2 le_rfl⟩

end AlgebraicNormality

reformulations.difference: The conclusion `IsAbsolutelyNormal x` unfolds to `NormalNumber.IsNormalInBase b x` for all b ≥ 2. That predicate reads digits only from `Int.fract x`, via `digitSeq b x n = ⌊b^(n+1) * Int.fract x⌋₊ % b`. So the integer-part digits are dropped. For negative x it reads the digits of {x} = 1 − {|x|}, which are the complements b−1−d of the digits of |x|. It also counts a word at every start position i < n, so an occurrence may run past the first n digits. Wikipedia and BC01 define normality on the full expansion S_{x,b}, with the integer part included and the radix point ignored. They count the word as a substring of the first n digits (BC01: positions j ≤ N+1−k).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (i) Let x be irrational and b ≥ 2. Then `digitSeq b (-x) n = b - 1 - digitSeq b x n`, because {−x} = 1 − {x} and b^(n+1)·{x} is not an integer. The map w ↦ b−1−w is a bijection on the words of each length k, so the two occurrence counts match word for word. Hence `IsNormalInBase b (-x) ↔ IsNormalInBase b x`, and so `IsNormalInBase b |x| ↔ IsNormalInBase b x`. Both hypotheses are invariant under negation (`IsAlgebraic.neg`, `Irrational.neg`), and 0 is not irrational. So the right-hand side is equivalent to its restriction to x > 0. (ii) Dropping the finite prefix of integer digits changes every occurrence count by at most (prefix length + k), which is o(n), so no limiting frequency changes. (iii) Counting by start position rather than by substring changes the count by at most k−1, which is also o(n). So for every irrational x the Lean predicate is exactly the sources' 'normal in base b', and the right-hand side is the sources' conjecture that every irrational algebraic number is absolutely normal. Proved in Lean (scratch file, no sorry, standard axioms only): `digitSeq_neg`, `isNormalInBase_neg_iff`, `isNormalInBase_abs_iff`, and the equivalence of this right-hand side with its restriction to positive x. Parts (ii) and (iii) are standard and were argued, not proved.

reformulations.difference: This uses the same `NormalNumber.IsNormalInBase` digit conventions: fractional-part digits only, complemented digits for negative x, and counting by start position.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Same argument as for `irrational_algebraic_absolutely_normal`, applied base by base. For irrational x and each b ≥ 2, the Lean 'normal in base b' is equivalent to the standard notion for |x|. So `∃ b ≥ 2, IsNormalInBase b x` is equivalent to the standard statement. I proved in Lean that the right-hand side is equivalent to its restriction to x > 0, using `isNormalInBase_neg_iff`. The required guard `2 ≤ b` is present. Without it the statement would be trivial: I proved that `IsNormalInBase 0 x` and `IsNormalInBase 1 x` hold for every real x.

sources_consulted: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number (raw wikitext via https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Normal_number&action=raw): 'It has also been conjectured that every irrational algebraic number is absolutely normal (which would imply that √2 is normal), and no counterexamples are known in any base. review.notes:
I checked all three declarations and found no misformalizations.

1. `irrational_algebraic_absolutely_normal`. This states exactly the conjecture in both cited sources and the Wikipedia List question ("Are all irrational algebraic numbers normal?"), where "normal" means absolutely normal. The polarity is affirmative, so this is not a negated conjecture. `research open` is correct: Wikipedia still says no irrational algebraic number has been proven normal in any base.

2. `irrational_algebraic_normal_in_some_base`. Neither source poses this ∀x∃b weakening verbatim. The file presents it as a weaker variant, and it is implied by the sources' conjecture. It is genuinely open: proving it would give the first proof that an irrational algebraic number, such as √2, is normal in some base. Refuting it would need an irrational algebraic number that is normal in no base, and Wikipedia says no counterexample is known in any base. Its docstring matches the Lean. The module docstring's "normal in any integer base" means "in some base", which the next sentence makes clear. The `2 ≤ b` guard is essential and present: I proved in Lean that `IsNormalInBase 0 x` and `IsNormalInBase 1 x` hold for every x.

3. `normal_in_some_base_of_absolutely_normal`. This is a correct API lemma, proved with standard axioms only.

Definition checks:
- `#print` confirms that `i + ↑j` is addition in ℕ (Fin.val coercion), not in Fin, and that the division is in ℝ.
- `digitSeq` gives the right digits: 1/4 in base 10 gives 2, 5, 0; −1/4 gives 7, from fract = 0.75.
- The k = 0 case is trivial (frequency 1 = 1/b^0).

`answer(sorry)` of type `Prop` elaborates to `True`, which is the repository convention.
